conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a well-studied set of 10 questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling during these first weeks and months with your new baby.  

Everything you share stays confidential within our team, and this is a judgment-free space. My goal is to support you, not to label you. We’ll move through the questions at your pace; each one asks about the past seven days, and we’ll keep the language conversational rather than clinical.  

When you’re ready, we can begin.  

First question: Over the last seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has even pleasant moments felt a bit flat or forced?

It’s strange… even the tiny “wins” feel muted. I used to love my morning coffee and scrolling through silly reels, but lately it’s like I’m watching someone else do it. When the baby gives me one of those sleepy milk-smiles, I think “this should feel amazing,” yet it lands as a quick flicker instead of real joy. I still try—play music, step outside for a minute—but most things feel flat, like the color’s been turned down.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Most days I can still laugh—like yesterday when my mom sent that goofy cat video—but it feels kind of forced. It’s like I hear myself chuckle and think, “Okay, that was funny,” yet the laughter fades fast and I’m right back to the heavy feeling in my chest.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to plan little things—like tomorrow’s walk to the coffee shop or ordering a new book—but the excitement fizzles before it even arrives. I still go through the motions, hoping the spark will come back, but mostly it feels like I’m just marking time rather than actually looking forward to anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s extra fussy, I immediately think it’s because I ate something wrong or didn’t read his cues fast enough. Last night he wouldn’t settle after his feeding and I kept replaying everything I might’ve messed up—maybe I didn’t burp him long enough, maybe I’m just not good at this. My partner says I’m too hard on myself, but the guilt just pops in before I can stop it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting on the couch, baby’s asleep, nothing’s actually wrong, but my chest feels tight like something bad’s about to happen. I check that he’s breathing over and over, and my mind jumps to these awful “what-ifs” even when there’s no real reason. I know it’s not logical, but I can’t shake the worry.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week I’ve gotten that sudden rush—heart racing, can’t catch my breath—like I’m about to bolt from the room, even though nothing’s happening. The worst was at 2 a.m. while I was folding laundry; my hands shook so hard I had to sit on them. It passes after a bit, but it leaves me jittery the rest of the night.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days it feels like the minute I finish one thing—diaper, feeding, laundry—two more pile up. I’ll look around the living room and just want to sit on the floor and cry because I can’t see how I’ll ever get it all done. I manage, mostly, but it’s like I’m wading through thick mud just to keep us both fed and clean.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… even when the baby’s asleep, my brain won’t shut off. I lie there replaying every little thing I think I did wrong, and the sadness feels heavy in my chest. Some nights I finally drift off around three, then I jerk awake at four, heart pounding, already worrying about the next day.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time, honestly. I wake up with this dull ache in my chest, and it just lingers. I’ll look at the baby and feel like I should be glowing, but instead there’s this gray cloud that won’t lift. I keep hoping tomorrow will feel lighter, but so far it hasn’t.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened three times this week. Yesterday I burst into tears while folding onesies—no real trigger, just this wave of sadness that overflowed. The littlest thing can set me off, and once I start it’s hard to stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that. I feel low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my baby deserves.

You've shared that over the past week most moments feel muted: laughter feels forced, excitement evaporates before it begins, and a persistent "gray cloud" of sadness makes even simple tasks feel like wading through mud. Crying arrives without warning, worry and sudden panic jolt you at night, and guilt floods in whenever the baby fusses. Yet you remain determined to be the mom your baby deserves and you deny any wish to harm yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 22, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>She can still laugh on most days, but describes it as "forced" and short-lived, matching "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent loss of anticipatory pleasure; excitement consistently fades, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient self-describes frequent, automatic self-blame for routine infant fussiness, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily anxiety with physical symptoms and intrusive thoughts without triggers, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes classic panic attacks occurring multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She describes feeling overwhelmed and tearful, but still managing basic tasks, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to persistent unhappiness and rumination, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly says "Most of the time" and describes persistent sadness, matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms crying multiple times in the past week, consistent with "quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 22 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale falls well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depressive symptoms. The patient endorses core DSM-5 criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness/guilt, psychomotor retardation, and insomnia. Ancillary symptoms of <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic</sym> are common in postpartum presentations and heighten functional impairment. No self-harm ideation is endorsed on Q10. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent evaluation with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary-care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med>
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, peer support groups, or <med>sertraline</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Share results with your partner or trusted support person so they can help coordinate appointments and household tasks
4. Practice 15-20 min daily of gentle movement or outdoor time; start with 5 min if fatigue is high
5. Use 4-7-8 breathing or a brief grounding exercise when panic sensations start
6. Encourage at least one 3-4 hour block of uninterrupted sleep per 24 h; consider partner/family night shift or pumped milk
7. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 22: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother (self-report)

Symptoms / behavioral indicators endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, “gray cloud,” daily sadness (Q8)  
- Marked anhedonia—laughter feels forced, excitement “fizzles” (Q1, Q2)  
- Frequent crying spells without clear trigger (Q9)  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Recurrent, intrusive worries and “what-ifs,” chest tightness (Q4)  
- Sudden panic-like episodes (heart racing, breathlessness, shaking) several ×/week, no situational trigger (Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “wading through mud,” difficulty coping with routine tasks (Q6)  
- Sleep initiation/maintenance problems linked to rumination and low mood (Q7)

Patterns / risk factors of screening significance  
- Symptoms present “most days” for ≥2 weeks  
- Functional impact evident (household tasks, enjoyment of infant)  
- No current thoughts of self-harm (Q10)  
- No prior psychiatric hx reported in this screen

Screening impression  
Responses are consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depressive symptoms with comorbid anxiety features; no acute safety concerns identified today. Recommend further clinical evaluation to determine diagnostic impression and treatment options.
